claims.claim: The CNBD and the pore domain must change conformation together, in a concerted way.
claims.source: We propose that when ligand binds to the isolated CNBD, the binding energy is sufficient to activate it and change its conformation, but it is not enough to activate the CNBD when it is part of the full-length channel, suggesting that the CNBD and the pore domain must change conformation together, in a concerted way.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The absence of a local conformational change in the binding pocket despite the bound ligand can be understood in the context of a concerted Monod-Wyman-Changeux (MWC) model.
claims.source: The absence of a local conformational change in the binding pocket despite the bound ligand can thus be understood in the context of a concerted Monod-Wyman-Changeux (Monod et al., 1965) (MWC) model, previously proposed to describe the gating of CNG/HCN channels and other multi-subunit ligand-gated ion channels (Li et al., 1997; Colquhoun and Sivilotti, 2004; Lape et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data in the context of an established theoretical model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The MWC model stipulates that the channel exists in two conformations: closed (or resting), and open (or activated).
claims.source: This model stipulates that the channel exists in two conformations: closed (or resting), and open (or activated) (Figure 8E, top).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MWC model.

claims.claim: All closed conformations, whether apo or ligand bound, are identical, differing only in the number of ligands bound.
claims.source: All closed conformations, whether apo or ligand bound, are identical, differing only in the number of ligands bound (all squares in Figure 8E, top).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MWC model as applied to the data.

claims.claim: Each closed channel can undergo a concerted conformational change to an open channel, meaning that all subunits undergo the closed to open transition at the same time.
claims.source: Each closed channel can undergo a concerted conformational change to an open channel, meaning that all subunits undergo the closed to open transition at the same time.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MWC model.

claims.claim: All open conformations are identical to each other.
claims.source: All open conformations are also identical to each other (all circles in Figure 8E, top).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MWC model.

claims.claim: The MWC model requires that the difference between partial agonists and full agonists lies only in the efficacy with which the agonist can induce the concerted conformational change.
claims.source: This model requires that the difference between partial agonists and full agonists lies only in the efficacy with which the agonist can induce the concerted conformational change (the vertical transition from all squares to all circles in Figure 8E, top).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MWC model.

claims.claim: The data shows identical, closed structures for the apo and inefficacious, partial agonist-bound SthK channels, which is consistent with the concerted gating model.
claims.source: Our data shows identical, closed structures for the apo and inefficacious, partial agonist-bound SthK channels, which is consistent with the concerted gating model (the functional states - closed - that we solved with cryo-EM are indicated by dashed green circles in Figure 8E, top).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data in support of the MWC model.

claims.claim: Identical structures are not expected from ion channels gating according to the sequential (or Koshland-Nemethy-Filmer, KNF) model.
claims.source: In contrast, identical structures are not expected from ion channels gating according to the sequential (or Koshland-Nemethy-Filmer, KNF [Koshland et al., 1966]) model, which predicts that binding of partial agonists and full agonists will induce specific closed conformational states (the red and green ligands leading to circles and octagons, respectively in Figure 8E, bottom), different than the apo state (squares) and perhaps different from each other (circles versus octagons in Figure 8E), leading to channel opening.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the sequential model and how it differs from the observed data, supported by citation and figure reference.

claims.claim: No major differences were found between the subunits within the tetramer when the structural data was processed without fourfold symmetrization.
claims.source: Further ruling out the sequential model, we found no major differences between the subunits within the tetramer when the structural data was processed without fourfold symmetrization (Figure 7A–C)
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the results of structural data processing shown in Figure 7A-C.

claims.claim: All ligands were bound to an occupancy close to 1 in each of the subunits within the tetramer.
claims.source: and all ligands were bound to an occupancy close to 1 in each of the subunits within the tetramer (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 7D-E.

claims.claim: Previous functional investigations employed concerted, sequential, or a combination of both models to describe gating in CNG and HCN channels.
claims.source: Previous functional investigations employed concerted, sequential, or a combination of both models to describe gating in CNG and HCN channels (Biskup et al., 2007; Li et al., 1997; Ulens and Siegelbaum, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: This study provides the first structural evidence that a concerted step exists in the gating of CNG channels.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this study provides the first structural evidence that a concerted step exists in the gating of CNG channels.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claims.claim: Other ligand-gated channels, such as the AMPA receptors, have been proposed to gate according to the sequential model.
claims.source: Conversely, other ligand-gated channels, such as the AMPA receptors, have been proposed to gate according to the sequential model, based on findings that the structures of the ligand binding domains display major differences depending on the type of agonist/antagonist bound (Armstrong and Gouaux, 2000; Armstrong et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2003; Sobolevsky et al., 2009; Twomey et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about other channels, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The lack of subconductance states observed at the single-channel level and the equal single-channel amplitudes when the channel opens in response to cAMP or cGMP-binding provide additional evidence for concerted channel gating.
claims.source: Additional evidence frequently invoked to support concerted channel gating and that we also found for SthK are the lack of subconductance states observed at the single-channel level and the equal single-channel amplitudes when the channel opens in response to cAMP or cGMP-binding (Figure 1E, Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is functional evidence supporting the concerted model, shown in figures.

claims.claim: There is only one structurally distinct open state.
claims.source: This suggests that there is only one structurally distinct open state, with the caveats that we are not able to observe states shorter than the dead time of the recording (~180 µs) and that structurally distinct open channel conformations may display the same single-channel current amplitude.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from functional data with acknowledgment of limitations.

claims.claim: There is only one 'activated' CNBD conformation reported by the crystal structures of the isolated CNBDs of SthK.
claims.source: Furthermore, in addition to the single 'resting' CNBD conformation reported here for SthK, there is also only one 'activated' CNBD conformation reported by the crystal structures of the isolated CNBDs of SthK (where the cAMP-bound is identical to the cGMP-bound conformation (Kesters et al., 2015), despite their quite different phenotypes at the functional level).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous structural data, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The CNBDs in the full-length apo HCN1 channel appear to be almost identical to those in the cAMP-bound HCN1, which are in the same 'activated' conformation seen in other CNBDs.
claims.source: In contrast to what we observe with SthK, the CNBDs in the full-length apo HCN1 channel appear to be almost identical to those in the cAMP-bound HCN1, which are in the same 'activated' conformation seen in other CNBDs (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative structural observation supported by citation and figure reference.

claims.claim: In HCN1, cAMP binding does not lead to a drastic conformational change likely because the CNBDs are already 'pre-activated' in the absence of ligand.
claims.source: Thus, in HCN1, cAMP binding does not lead to a drastic conformational change likely because the CNBDs are already 'pre-activated' in the absence of ligand.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from structural observations.

claims.claim: The pre-activation of HCN1 CNBDs is in agreement with functional data showing that cAMP binding has minimal effect on HCN1 channel activity and that they are the fastest activating HCN channels.
claims.source: This is in agreement with functional data showing not only that cAMP binding has minimal effect on HCN1 channel activity but also that they are the fastest activating HCN channels, requiring the least amount of hyperpolarization for opening (Santoro et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a correlation between structural observations and functional properties, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The full-length structure of TAX-4 is used as a proxy for open SthK.
claims.source: However, based on the near identity structure-wise between the 'activated' CNBD structures of SthK (Kesters et al., 2015) and TAX-4 (Li et al., 2017) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we will use the full-length structure of TAX-4, the only open cGMP-bound CNG structure, as a proxy for open SthK.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological decision based on structural similarity, supported by citations and figure reference.

claims.claim: In TAX-4, the CNBD/C-linker domains are closer to the membrane, and are rotated outwards, ~9 degrees counterclockwise viewed from the extracellular side compared to SthK apo.
claims.source: In TAX-4, the CNBD/C-linker domains are closer to the membrane, and are rotated outwards, ~9 degrees counterclockwise viewed from the extracellular side compared to SthK apo (Figure 8C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 8C-D.

claims.claim: Movements of the C-linker can be transmitted to the S4-S5 linker of the adjacent subunit due to direct interactions between these regions.
claims.source: Movements of the C-linker can also be transmitted to the S4-S5 linker of the adjacent subunit due to direct interactions between these regions (dashed circle Figure 8A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a structural observation with inference about functional coupling, shown in Figure 8A,B.

claims.claim: Displacements of the S5 transmembrane helix can be directly sensed by the pore helix and selectivity filter, a putative gate for these channels, and bias its opening.
claims.source: Displacements of the S5 transmembrane helix can be directly sensed by the pore helix and selectivity filter, a putative gate for these channels (Flynn and Zagotta, 2001), and bias its opening (Mazzolini et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural considerations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The direct interaction between the S4-S5 linker and the CNBD provides a direct link between cAMP binding and voltage sensor moving and may explain channel modulation by voltage.
claims.source: Additionally, this direct interaction between the S4-S5 linker and the CNBD also provides a direct link between cAMP binding and voltage sensor moving and may explain channel modulation by voltage.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The conformations of apo, cAMP-bound and cGMP-bound SthK are identical, and functionally correspond to resting/closed states.
claims.source: We report here the cryo-EM structures of apo, cAMP-bound and cGMP-bound SthK potassium channels in lipid nanodiscs. The conformations are identical, and functionally correspond to resting/closed states as indicated by single-channel recordings of SthK.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings combining structural and functional data.

claims.claim: Identical apo, and partial agonist-bound conformations indicate that SthK gating can be described with a concerted model, with strong coupling between the ligand-binding and pore domains.
claims.source: Identical apo, and partial agonist-bound conformations indicate that SthK gating can be described with a concerted model, with strong coupling between the ligand-binding and pore domains.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the structural data.

claims.claim: The strong discrimination against cGMP in SthK is hypothesized to be based on its preferred binding configuration to the apo conformation which differs from the configuration that leads to channel activation.
claims.source: We hypothesize that the strong discrimination against cGMP in SthK is based on its preferred binding configuration to the apo conformation which differs from the configuration that leads to channel activation.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on structural observations.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on cyclic nucleotide-modulated ion channels, describing their physiological roles in visual/olfactory signal transduction and cardiac/neuronal pacemaking, their classification into CNG and HCN subfamilies in eukaryotes, and the existence of prokaryotic homologs. These channels are activated by cAMP/cGMP binding to cytoplasmic CNBDs, leading to changes in membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C14 establish well-documented background knowledge about cyclic nucleotide-modulated channels, supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These are standard introductory statements that accurately reflect the current understanding of the field.

results.result: Prior structural work on HCN1 and TAX-4 provided limited conformational states, and existing structures are insufficient to distinguish between concerted (MWC) and sequential (KNF) gating models due to lack of correspondence between structural conformations and functional states.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C24 accurately summarize prior structural work and identify the knowledge gap that motivates this study. The assessment that existing structures are insufficient to distinguish gating mechanisms is a reasonable evaluation of the literature, supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: SthK is a prokaryotic cyclic nucleotide-modulated channel from Spirochaeta thermophila that shares ~35% sequence similarity with eukaryotic CNG channels and is more functionally similar to CNG than HCN channels. It is amenable to both high-resolution structural and single-channel functional studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28, C33-C34 establish SthK as the experimental system, supported by citations to previous work. The sequence similarity is quantified (C27) and the functional similarity to CNG channels is documented (C26). The suitability for structural and functional studies is supported by prior publications.

results.result: Functional characterization shows that purified SthK is inactive without cyclic nucleotides, becomes active upon cAMP addition with activity enhanced by depolarization, and shows no inactivation. cAMP is a partial agonist (Po < 1 even at saturating concentrations), while cGMP is an extremely poor partial agonist (not an antagonist as previously reported), showing infrequent openings.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C45 describe functional properties supported by single-channel recordings (Figures 1, 4) and citations to previous work. The reclassification of cGMP from antagonist to poor partial agonist (C44) is supported by observation of infrequent openings (C43, Figure 1E). The explanation for discrepancy with prior work (C45) is reasonable speculation.

results.result: Three cryo-EM structures of SthK (apo, cAMP-bound, cGMP-bound) were solved to similar resolutions (3.42-3.46 Å). The apo structure represents the first apo resting state of a CNG family member. Unexpectedly, ligand-bound structures display apo-like, resting CNBDs despite bound ligands, with very small RMSDs between all three structures (0.40-0.50 Å).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 describe the main structural findings. Resolution values are quantified (C46), the novelty of the apo structure is stated (C47, C29), and the unexpected similarity between apo and ligand-bound states is documented with RMSD values (C50). These are supported by the structural data presented in Figures 1-2 and supplementary figures.

results.result: SthK displays a traditional potassium channel pore architecture with a TIGYGD selectivity filter. The pore is constricted at I215 in the middle of the cavity but widens toward the intracellular side rather than forming a bundle crossing. The gate may be located at this mid-cavity constriction, though a selectivity filter gate cannot be excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 describe the pore architecture supported by structural data (Figure 3) and comparisons to other K+ channels. The proposal that the gate is at I215 (C57) is appropriately presented as speculation based on structural observations. The acknowledgment of alternative gating mechanisms (C58) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: SthK contains a voltage sensor-like domain with 4 basic residues in S4, of which R111 and K114 are positioned within the membrane electric field and likely contribute to gating charge. L54 in S2 is proposed as the charge transfer center. The voltage sensor is likely in the resting conformation in the structures (0 mV on EM grid). The strength of interactions between S4 charges and countercharges correlates with voltage dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C71 describe the voltage sensor domain with structural evidence (Figure 4A) and functional correlation (Figure 4B-C). The inference that the voltage sensor is in the resting state (C69) is well-reasoned based on 0 mV conditions and functional data showing activation at ~85 mV. The correlation between interaction strength and voltage dependence (C71) is supported by comparative analysis.

results.result: Multiple lipid molecules (POPG) were resolved binding to SthK transmembrane helices, predominantly in the top leaflet. Lipids bind at subunit interfaces and between voltage sensors and pore domains. Only one lipid was identified in the inner leaflet, bound along S6 near the gate region. These lipid interactions may facilitate voltage gating and are consistent with lipid-dependent gating.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 describe lipid-protein interactions supported by structural data (Figure 5). The assignment of densities to POPG lipids (C72) is reasonable given the nanodisc composition. The asymmetric distribution (C73) and functional implications (C74, C77) are appropriately presented as inferences supported by previous functional data (Schmidpeter et al., 2018). Comparison to other channels (C80) provides context.

results.result: The C-linker/CNBD domain of SthK is homologous to other cyclic nucleotide-modulated channels but differs in C-helix position. In all full-length SthK structures (apo and ligand-bound), the C-helix is swung away from the binding pocket in a 'resting' conformation, unlike the 'activated' conformation seen in isolated CNBD crystal structures. Ligand presence is confirmed by experimental and difference maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 describe a key structural finding supported by Figure 6 and comparisons to crystal structures. The demonstration of ligand presence via difference maps (C84-C85) addresses potential concerns about ligand occupancy. This is a critical observation for the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: cAMP was modeled in an anti configuration though the density can accommodate syn. cGMP was modeled in syn configuration, favored by interaction with T378 and the 95:5 syn:anti solution distribution. Both conformers of cAMP likely bind (70:30 distribution), while cGMP binds predominantly in syn to SthK.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 describe ligand binding modes supported by density maps (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and known solution properties of cyclic nucleotides. The modeling decisions are appropriately justified by map quality, specific interactions (T378-cGMP), and solution conformer distributions. The inference about mixed cAMP binding (C90) is reasonable.

results.result: Analysis of unsymmetrized (C1) structures shows ligand occupancy close to 1 in all four subunits for both cAMP and cGMP, with no major differences between subunits within the tetramer.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C122-C123 are supported by C1 refinement analysis shown in Figure 7. The demonstration of full occupancy in all subunits and lack of asymmetry provides important evidence against sequential gating models. The analysis is appropriate and well-documented.

results.result: The ligand-bound structures correspond to closed states based on functional data showing low open probability at 0 mV (the condition on EM grids): Po ~0.05-0.1 for cAMP-bound channels, meaning at most 5-10% of channels are open. 3D classification did not detect an open state class.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 establish the functional state assignment for the structures, critical for mechanistic interpretation. The reasoning is sound: combining Po measurements at different voltages (Figure 4) with knowledge of conditions on EM grids (0 mV) to estimate the proportion of open channels. The failure to detect open states in 3D classification (C97) supports the conclusion.

results.result: The partial agonist effect of cAMP may be explained by mixed-configuration binding: only anti-cAMP can lead to activation (syn clashes with the activated CNBD), so only a subset of cAMP binding events (~70%) can promote opening. In HCN2, where cAMP is efficacious, syn-cAMP may not clash due to different C-helix composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 propose a mechanism for cAMP partial agonism based on structural modeling (C100, Figure 6D-E insert). While the structural observations of clashes are supported, the quantitative link between 70% anti-cAMP binding and the observed Po (~0.2-0.5) is not rigorously established. The proposal is plausible but requires additional validation. The speculation about HCN2 (C102) is reasonable comparative analysis.

results.result: cGMP is a very poor partial agonist (Po ~0.003) because the resting CNBD preferentially binds syn-cGMP (favored by T378 interaction and 95:5 solution distribution), but syn-cGMP cannot be accommodated in the activated CNBD due to clash with L422. This differs from TAX-4 and HCN2 where syn-cGMP stabilizes the activated state.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 propose a mechanism for cGMP discrimination supported by structural observations (Figure 6E insert showing clash), functional data (Figure 1E showing Po ~0.003), and comparative analysis with other channels. The mechanism is internally consistent and explains the functional observations. The comparison to TAX-4 and HCN2 (C108) is supported by citations.

results.result: Ligand binding to full-length SthK does not induce the conformational changes seen in isolated CNBDs, indicating strong allosteric coupling between CNBD and pore. The data support a concerted (MWC) gating model where all closed states are identical regardless of ligand occupancy, and channels transition concertedly to open states. This is inconsistent with sequential (KNF) models that predict ligand-specific closed conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C121 present the central mechanistic conclusion. The evidence is strong: identical structures for apo and ligand-bound states (C50, C120), full ligand occupancy in all subunits (C92), no subunit asymmetry (C122), and appropriate functional state assignment (C93-C98). The interpretation in terms of MWC model (C114-C120) is well-reasoned and supported by the data. The contrast with KNF predictions (C121) is clearly articulated.

results.result: This study provides the first structural evidence for concerted gating in CNG channels. Additional supporting evidence includes lack of subconductance states, equal single-channel amplitudes for cAMP and cGMP activation, and only one activated CNBD conformation in isolated domain structures despite different functional effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C129 contextualize the findings and provide additional supporting evidence. The claim of novelty (C125) is appropriate given the structural evidence. The functional evidence (C127: no subconductance, equal amplitudes) supports concerted gating, though the caveats about temporal resolution (C128) are appropriately noted. The observation about isolated CNBD structures (C129) provides additional support.

results.result: In contrast to SthK, HCN1 CNBDs appear pre-activated in both apo and cAMP-bound states, explaining why cAMP has minimal functional effect and why HCN1 channels are the fastest activating HCN channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 provide comparative analysis with HCN1, supported by structural comparison (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and functional data from literature (C132, citing Santoro et al., 1998). This comparison strengthens the interpretation of SthK results and explains functional differences between channel types.

results.result: Using TAX-4 as a proxy for open SthK, the proposed activation mechanism involves CNBD/C-linker domains moving closer to the membrane and rotating ~9° counterclockwise. C-linker movements are transmitted to the S4-S5 linker of adjacent subunits and then to S5, which can influence the pore helix and selectivity filter gate. This provides a link between cAMP binding and voltage sensor movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 propose an activation mechanism based on comparison to TAX-4 structure (Figure 8). While the use of TAX-4 as a proxy is justified by CNBD structural similarity (C133), this is indirect evidence. The proposed conformational changes (C134) and coupling mechanisms (C135-C137) are reasonable inferences from structural comparisons but lack direct experimental validation for SthK. The mechanism is plausible but speculative.

results.result: The main conclusions are that apo, cAMP-bound, and cGMP-bound SthK structures are identical closed/resting states, indicating concerted gating with strong CNBD-pore coupling. Ligand discrimination is proposed to result from different preferred binding configurations (syn vs anti) in resting versus activated states.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 summarize the main findings. The structural identity (C138) is well-supported by data. The concerted gating conclusion (C139) is strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence. The ligand discrimination mechanism (C140) is supported by structural observations though some aspects remain hypothetical. Overall, these conclusions are well-supported by the presented data.

results.result: The study presents cryo-EM structures of SthK in three states that correspond to defined functional states (no, moderate, and low activity), representing the first apo resting structure of a CNG family member. The structural similarity despite different ligands indicates strong allosteric coupling and concerted gating. Different ligand orientations in resting versus activated structures suggest a mechanism for ligand discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C29-C32 represent the core findings stated in the abstract and introduction. These are well-supported by the combination of structural data (Figures 1-2, 6-7) and functional data (Figures 1E, 4) that allow assignment of functional states to structures. The novelty claims (C29) and mechanistic proposals (C6, C7, C31, C32) are supported by the data presented, though some mechanistic details remain to be fully validated.
